claims.text: Premelting and melting behavior in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is primarily governed by competition between composition-dependent mixing enthalpy and configurational entropy.
Enthalpy-driven interatomic interactions can promote phase segregation or phase stabilization.
Configurational entropy favors a homogeneous alloy phase.
A more negative effective mixing enthalpy delays the onset of premelting.
A more negative effective mixing enthalpy raises nanoparticle melting temperature.
A less negative effective mixing enthalpy causes premelting at lower temperatures.
Slight compositional changes can systematically modulate mixing enthalpy while retaining high-entropy character.
Differences in mixing enthalpy induce changes in local atomic arrangements and short-range order.
Changes in local atomic arrangements and short-range order affect the initiation of surface liquefaction and bulk melting.
More negative mixing enthalpy corresponds to stronger interatomic bonding in the proposed nanoparticle compositions.
Stronger interatomic bonding increases the energy barrier for atomic mobility.
An increased barrier to atomic mobility delays premelting and raises the melting temperature.
A less negative mixing enthalpy lowers the barrier to atomic mobility and facilitates earlier surface disorder.
The predicted enthalpy-dependent trend should hold for high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles approximately 5–20 nm in size.
Surface-to-volume effects are significant for nanoparticles in the proposed 5–20 nm range.
Extreme changes in composition or particle size may introduce governing factors outside the proposed enthalpy–entropy competition.
Earlier literature has correlated an enthalpy–entropy mixing framework with phase selection.
Synthesis defects, surface energies, and nanoparticle morphology may influence the relationship between mixing enthalpy and melting behavior.
